title: The many faces of Oidípous
description: From Greek to Unicode: why Oidípous is more than a domain name.

body:
# The many faces of Oidípous

No important name has only one face. **Oidípous** appears as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in turn: the name and its roots, the Greek original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in a browser. Taken together, those faces explain why *oidipous* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Oidípous
- **ASCII form:** oidipous
- **Meaning:** "Swollen-foot (from οἰδάω + πούς)"
- **Domain of influence:** Fate, Riddles, Thebes
- **Pantheon:** Greek
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** Οἰδίπους (Greek)
- **Live domain:** oidipous.com

## Overview

**Oidípous** (*oidipous*) — Fate, Riddles, Thebes · Swollen-foot (from οἰδάω + πούς) — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Fate, Riddles, Thebes". The name means "Swollen-foot (from οἰδάω + πούς)".

**Oidípous** belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is associated with fate, riddles, thebes.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Oidípous** and serves its temple at [oidipous.com](https://punicodex.com/oidipous/). The original preserves a prosodic feature — stress — that ASCII loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *oidipous* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Greek as **Οἰδίπους**. Etymologically it means "Swollen-foot (from οἰδάω + πούς)".

The reconstructed proto-form is *h₁eyd-* (proto-indo-european, "to swell"). Greek Οἰδίπους 'swollen-foot', from οἰδάω 'to swell' and πούς 'foot'; the name encodes the injury inflicted on the infant exposed by his parents.

The ASCII form *oidipous* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Oidípous** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves a prosodic feature — stress — that ASCII loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **o** → **O** — Omicron
- **i** → **i** — Iota
- **d** → **d** — Delta
- **i** → **í** — Acute on iota
- **p** → **p** — Pi
- **o** → **o** — Omicron
- **u** → **u** — Upsilon
- **s** → **s** — Sigma

The canonical temple for this name is served at **oidipous.com**.

## Etymology & Roots

The recorded derivation reads: Greek Οἰδίπους 'swollen-foot', from οἰδάω 'to swell' and πούς 'foot'; the name encodes the injury inflicted on the infant exposed by his parents.

The reconstructed proto-form is **h₁eyd-* (proto-indo-european), glossed as "to swell".

The reconstruction is classed as attested.

## The Original Script

The name is written in Greek as **Οἰδίπους**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *oidipous* and the PuniCodex restoration **Oidípous** are measured: the restoration preserves its pitch accent of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/oidipous/** — Greek Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **O** — Initial character of the restored form Oidípous.
- **idípous** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Greek tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'OIDIPOUS' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — Oidípous, the restored Unicode form of the name

Oidípous is Tier 1 because the Greek form preserves a distinctive prosodic feature that ASCII loses — stress — and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists.

## Mythology

The stories of **Oidípous** circulate within the Greek corpus, where the figure embodies fate, riddles, thebes.

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Oidípous is attested in the canonical Greek sources as a figure associated with fate, riddles, thebes.

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "Swollen-foot (from οἰδάω + πούς)" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Oidípous** is the Theban king destined to kill his father and marry his mother. The Sphinx blocks Thebes until Oedipus solves her riddle; his reward is the throne and a marriage that fulfills the oracle's curse. Sophocles's *Oedipus Tyrannus* dramatizes the slow uncovering of this truth, making Oedipus the model of human knowledge that discovers its own blindness. The plague that strikes Thebes at the play's opening is understood as pollution caused by the unsolved murder of Laius, forcing Oedipus to hunt down himself.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Oidípous concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Restored Name** — The Unicode form Oidípous carries the original marks of the Greek tradition.
- **Source Script** — Attested in the original script as Οἰδίπους.
- **Domain** — Fate, Riddles, Thebes
- **Etymology** — Swollen-foot (from οἰδάω + πούς)

Oidípous is shown with the **Sphinx** at his feet, the riddle solved; later images add the **swollen ankles** marked by pins. On Attic vases he is often a mature king, while Hellenistic and Roman art prefers the blinded wanderer led by Antigone.

The contrast between solver and victim is the visual core of his myth.

## Epithets & Cult Titles

Oidípous is defined by epithets of pain and knowledge: **οἰδίπους** (*oidipous*, "swollen-foot") records the piercing of his infant ankles; **λυτήρ** (*lytēr*, "riddler") marks his defeat of the Sphinx; and **μητρολέκτης** (*mētrolektēs*, "mother-marriage") names his tragic transgression. Thebes called him **παῖς Λαΐου** (*pais Laiou*, son of Laius).

Every epithet is a plot summary, binding name to destiny.

## The Homeric Hymns

Oidípous does not appear in the Homeric Hymns, but the **Odyssey** places him among the great sinners in the underworld, already famous for the parricide and incest that define his legend. The Theban cycle, of which Oedipus is the central figure, predates the extant hymns and shaped their audience's understanding of fate.

The absence of a hymn to Oedipus is itself significant: his story belongs to tragedy, not cult praise.

## Oracle Sites & Sanctuaries

The oracle of **Apollo at Delphi** sets Oidípous's tragedy in motion: Laius is told that his son will kill him, and Oedipus later learns there that he is the polluter of Thebes. The Pythias ambiguous pronouncements operate as the mechanism of fate in the Sophoclean drama.

Delphi is therefore the unseen stage-manager of the entire Theban cycle.

Oidípous appears within the Greek tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

## Cultural Legacy

Oidípous continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Greek tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes. Freud's "Oedipus complex" made the name foundational for twentieth-century psychology, while the plays remain central to Western theater.

## A Meditation

Oidípous embodies fate, riddles, thebes in the Greek imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make the figure recognizable in the source tradition.

## The Unicode Restoration

Oidípous is classified as **Tier 1**: the original carries both stress and length, and only one valid Unicode restoration exists. The ASCII fallback *oidipous* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the 8 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 1: 1 mark of stress (í). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **oidipous.com**. Behind the scenes the DNS carries it in punycode form — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Oidípous; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Greek can now be typed into any browser on earth.

Myth, script, sound, cult, legacy, domain: the faces of Oidípous add up to a single argument — that a name is a record, and records deserve fidelity. ## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Oidípous**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *oidipous* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 8 characters, 7 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **o** stays as it is — Omicron.

The **i** stays as it is — Iota.

The **d** stays as it is — Delta.

The **i** becomes **í** — Acute on iota.

The **p** stays as it is — Pi.

The **o** stays as it is — Omicron.

The **u** stays as it is — Upsilon.

The **s** stays as it is — Sigma.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.
